questions.q: What is the best-case time complexity of Insertion Sort for an already sorted array?
questions.explanation: In the best case (already sorted), Insertion Sort only makes one comparison for each element and no shifts, resulting in linear time complexity $O(n)$.

questions.q: ...........is a contiguous area of memory consisting of equal-size elements.
questions.explanation: An array is defined as a collection of elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory locations.

questions.q: What is the access time required to retrieve the element located at position (5,9) in a 7-row and 12-column array?
questions.explanation: Using row-major ordering for a 1-indexed array: $Address = Base + size \times ((row - 1) \times total\_columns + (col - 1))$. Here, rows=7, cols=12, target=(5,9).

questions.q: The complexity of adding three elements to the end of an array is.......
questions.explanation: Adding a constant number of elements (like 3) to the end of an array is a constant time operation, $O(1)$, assuming the array has sufficient capacity.

questions.q: If `tail == head`, this means the linked list is empty?
questions.explanation: False. If `head == tail` and they are not null, the list contains exactly one element. An empty list is typically represented by `head == null`.

questions.q: `Find(Key)` in a double linked list with a tail is:
questions.explanation: To find a specific key in a linked list (single or double), you must perform a linear search from the head (or tail), which takes $O(n)$ time.

questions.q: `AddAfter(Node, Key)` in a single linked list with a tail is:
questions.explanation: Since the specific `Node` is already provided, adding a new node after it only requires updating a few pointers, which is $O(1)$.

questions.q: `Erase(Key)` in a single linked list with a tail is....
questions.explanation: In a single linked list, even if you find the key, you need a pointer to the *previous* node to remove it. This requires traversing the list, making it $O(n)$.

questions.q: `TopBack()` in a single linked list with a tail is:
questions.explanation: With a tail pointer, accessing the last element (TopBack) is a direct operation taking $O(1)$ time.

questions.q: Which operation removes and returns the first added key?
questions.explanation: Removing the first added key (First-In, First-Out) is the definition of the `Dequeue` operation in a Queue.

questions.q: Stack operations are known as..........
questions.explanation: Stacks follow the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle.

questions.q: `PushBack(Key)` in a single linked list without a tail is:
questions.explanation: Without a tail pointer, you must traverse the entire list from the head to reach the last node to append a new one, resulting in $O(n)$ complexity.

questions.q: To return and remove the most recently added key in a stack, we use the....... function.
questions.explanation: The `Pop()` operation in a stack removes and returns the most recently added (top) element.

questions.q: Stack operation `Push()` is implemented using LinkedList.......
questions.explanation: For a standard single linked list, `PushFront` is $O(1)$, making it the most efficient way to implement a Stack's `Push` operation.

questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of Linear Search?
questions.explanation: In the worst case, Linear Search must check every element in the list, resulting in $O(n)$ complexity.

questions.q: Which algorithm is adaptive and performs well on partially sorted arrays?
questions.explanation: Insertion Sort is adaptive; its performance improves significantly when the input array is already partially sorted.

questions.q: The complexity of adding an element to the middle of an array is:
questions.explanation: Adding an element to the middle requires shifting approximately half of the existing elements to make room, which is $O(n)$.

questions.q: Which operation checks if the stack has elements?
questions.explanation: The `Empty()` (or `isEmpty()`) operation returns a boolean indicating whether the stack contains any elements.

questions.q: When you apply `PushBack` in a Linked List that contains exactly one Node, you must update:
questions.explanation: If there is already one node, `head` already points to it. Adding a second node at the back requires updating the `tail` to point to this new last node.

questions.q: When applying `pop()` in a Stack implemented with an array, you should:
questions.explanation: Popping an element from an array-based stack involves decreasing the counter (`numElements`) that tracks the current top index.
